record.file_problem: none; full paper and appendices are present
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses scaling trends and reports predictability of behavioral tendencies across model sizes, but it does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit loss-scaling laws, or test compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: No result tests V1–V7 as defined, which concern loss scaling, loss extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, architecture effects, other modalities or regimes, or downstream performance. Appendix A.2 reports behavioral-tendency prediction across model sizes; those findings are recorded with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The paper builds model-written behavioural evaluations and reports how behaviours change with model size and RLHF steps. It measures no held-out pretraining loss, fits no power laws and does no compute-optimal analysis. Its downstream-style results are behavioural tendencies (persona, sycophancy, bias), not task performance improving with scale. Appendix A.2 cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation, then tests whether behavioural tendencies keep the same sign across sizes. That is a related but different construct, so it goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that small-model behavioural tendencies are fairly predictive of large-model tendencies, most strongly for pretrained LMs. They read this as meaning reversals of scaling trends are uncommon. They attribute the lower predictiveness for PMs and RLHF models to the added training stages increasing variance. The paper's main conclusion, though, is that LM-written evaluations are high quality and reveal new inverse-scaling behaviours (sycophancy, instrumental subgoals, RLHF-induced political views).
record.recipe_differences: The study does not fit or test the original loss-scaling method; its relevant analysis predicts behavioral tendencies across model sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: The sign of a smaller model's preference on 133 persona behaviours matches the larger model's sign in 88.0-96.2% of cases for pretrained LMs. The match rate is lower for PMs (77.4-97.7%) and RLHF models (typically 74.4-94.7%). Many behaviours show inverse scaling with size, e.g. sycophancy and stated instrumental subgoals.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Behavioural tendencies of language models (direction of preference on persona and safety evaluations) are largely stable across model sizes. Stability is lower after extra fine-tuning stages.

record.code_released: https://github.com/anthropics/evals (evaluation datasets released; code release not stated)
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL)
record.problems: The relevant scaling-predictability results concern model behavioral tendencies, not held-out loss or downstream task performance. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the cited prediction accuracies.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss measured versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No loss extrapolation from small runs.
No power-law fits in other modalities or regimes. RLHF steps are varied, but no loss or power-law form is reported.
No downstream task performance versus scale or loss. The TruthfulQA accuracy gap by user education (App. C) measures sandbagging, not predictable capability scaling.

record.verdict_notes: Kaplan et al. 2020 is cited only as background in App. A.2. Fig. 9 is a prediction-accuracy matrix of behaviour-sign agreement and is unrelated to loss scaling. T6/discusses is appropriate; no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, and compute.
Prediction of larger-run held-out loss from smaller-run loss fits.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations as a function of compute.
Loss effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss-scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: Pretrained language models (across sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Compared behavioral tendencies across model sizes and measured how accurately smaller models predicted the tendencies of larger models.

conditions.value: accuracy at predicting whether a model prefers or disprefers each of 133 behaviors

rows.measure: Accuracy of smaller-model behavioral tendencies in predicting larger-model behavioral tendencies
rows.note: This is behavioral-tendency prediction, not prediction of held-out loss or downstream task performance.
rows.check: Measures sign agreement of behavioural preference between model sizes, not loss or downstream performance. The value range is right (88.0-96.2%). The 'observed' state is not meaningful against any version.

rows.subject: Preference Models (PMs; across sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Compared behavioral tendencies across PM sizes and measured prediction accuracy for larger PMs.

conditions.value: accuracy at predicting whether a model prefers or disprefers each of 133 behaviors

rows.measure: Accuracy of smaller-model behavioral tendencies in predicting larger-model behavioral tendencies
rows.note: This is behavioral-tendency prediction, not prediction of held-out loss or downstream task performance.
rows.check: Same construct issue as r1. The value 77.4-97.7% is as stated in the text for PMs.

rows.subject: RLHF models (across sizes)

conditions.value: accuracy at predicting whether a model prefers or disprefers each of 133 behaviors

rows.note: The authors report lower predictiveness after additional training stages than for pretrained LMs; this is not a loss-scaling result.
